examples.analytical: Scholars often read the author's essays on music as a parergon to the novels, yet they reveal the theory behind the fiction.

nuance.analogy: A parergon is like the doodles in the margin of a notebook: they are not the main lesson, but they can reveal how the mind works.
nuance.etymology: From Greek parergon, 'work done beside, by-work', from para, 'beside', and ergon, 'work'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as 'gon' with a long vowel, as in 'GOHN'.
Using it in casual speech, where most Americans will not understand it.

parergon.etymology: From Ancient Greek *πάρεργον* (“subordinate or secondary business; by-work”), neuter of *πάρεργος* (“beside the main subject, subordinate, incidental”).

senses.definition: The term of office of a Christian patriarch.
senses.example: The patriarchate of Pope John Paul II as Patriarch of the West was more than 25 years.

senses.definition: A patriarchal system or community.
The office or ecclesial jurisdiction of such a patriarch.
senses.example: The Patriarchate of Constantinople has primacy over the whole of the Orthodox world.

senses.definition: The office-space occupied by a patriarch and his staff.
senses.example: The Latin patriarchate in Jerusalem is, by modern standards, a very cramped space.

core.definition: The office, term of office, or church area led by a patriarch, a senior bishop in some Christian churches.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PAY, with a lighter secondary stress on ARK. The final -ate is a reduced "it," not "ate."

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "patriarchate" mostly in church history, theology and news about Eastern Orthodox or Eastern Catholic churches. It is formal and rarely used in everyday talk. Protestants in the US do not use the term for their own leaders. When speaking casually, say "the patriarch's church" or "the patriarchal see."

distinctions.note: Patriarchy is a social system of male dominance, while patriarchate is a church office or jurisdiction under a patriarch.
A see is a bishop's diocese, while a patriarchate is a larger jurisdiction led by a patriarch.

examples.everyday: A friend mentioned the Ecumenical Patriarchate, and I had to look it up.
examples.professional: Our translation team coordinates with the regional patriarchate on the new liturgical texts.
examples.analytical: The claims of the Patriarchate of Constantinople rest on its historical primacy of honor among the Orthodox churches.

nuance.analogy: A patriarchate is like a regional headquarters: it is a large area of authority with a leader at the top.
nuance.etymology: From patriarch, from Greek patriarchēs, "father-ruler," with the suffix -ate for office or jurisdiction.
common_mistakes: Confusing "patriarchate" with "patriarchy."
Stressing the last syllable as "pa-tree-ar-KATE."

traditions.view: A patriarchate is a major self-governing church jurisdiction, led by a patriarch who holds a primacy of honor among the bishops.
Patriarchates are historic jurisdictions, mainly for Eastern Catholic churches, that remain under the authority of the Pope.
Most Protestant churches do not have patriarchates, so the term is mainly used in discussions of Eastern churches.

patriarchate.etymology: From Middle French *patriarcat*, from Old French *patriarcat*, from Medieval Latin *patriarchatus*, from Ancient Greek *πατριάρχης* (“patriarch”).

senses.definition: An excessive attention to detail or rules.
senses.example: I don’t want to listen to your pedantries anymore.

senses.definition: An instance of such behavior.
senses.example: I don’t want to listen to your pedantries anymore.

senses.definition: An overly ambitious display of learning.

core.definition: Excessive concern with minor rules or details, or a showy display of knowledge that irritates others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PED. The middle syllable is a weak schwa, and the final '-ry' is a clear 'tree' sound, not 'tri.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes fussiness or showy learning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'pedantry' in essays, reviews and serious discussions to name an excessive focus on technical correctness. In casual speech, people more often say 'pedantic' or 'nitpicking.' It is used more in writing than in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Nitpicking is informal and focuses on tiny faults; pedantry is more formal and may also involve showing off learning.
Scholarship is serious study with value; pedantry is an empty show of detail without much point.

examples.everyday: Getting into whether the store is technically a 'market' is just pedantry, so let's go eat.
examples.professional: Insisting on the old file naming convention is pedantry that slows the whole team down.
examples.analytical: The essay degenerates into pedantry when it catalogs every variant spelling and loses sight of the argument.

nuance.analogy: Pedantry is like polishing the back of a cabinet no one will ever see.
nuance.etymology: From 'pedant' plus the suffix '-ry,' from Italian 'pedante.'
common_mistakes: Using it for careful scholarship in a positive sense.
Stressing the last syllable as 'pe-DAN-tree.'

senses.definition: To remove the skin or outer covering of.
senses.example: I sat by my sister's bed, peeling oranges for her.

senses.definition: To remove something from the outer or top layer of.
senses.example: I peeled (the skin from) a banana and ate it hungrily.

senses.definition: To become detached, come away, especially in flakes or strips; to shed skin in such a way.
senses.example: I had been out in the sun too long, and my nose was starting to peel.

senses.definition: To remove one's clothing.
senses.example: The children peeled by the side of the lake and jumped in.

senses.definition: To move, separate (off or away).
senses.example: The scrum-half peeled off and made for the touchlines.

senses.definition: To play a peel shot.
To send through a hoop (of a ball other than one's own).
The skin or outer layer of a fruit, vegetable, etc.
The action of peeling away from a formation.
A cosmetic preparation designed to remove dead skin or to exfoliate.
A shovel or similar instrument, now especially a pole with a flat disc at the end used for removing pizza or loaves of bread from a baker's oven.
A T-shaped implement used by printers and bookbinders for hanging wet sheets of paper on lines or poles to dry.
A takeout which removes a stone from play as well as the delivered stone.

core.definition: To remove the skin or outer covering of a fruit, vegetable or similar food.

pronunciation.tip: This is a single syllable with a long 'ee' vowel. Don't add a 'uh' after the 'l,' and make the final 'l' clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a routine kitchen task.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'peel the potatoes' or 'peel an orange' in everyday cooking. 'Peel off' is common for removing clothing or stickers, and 'peel out' means to accelerate quickly in a car. The noun 'peel' is used for the skin, as in 'lemon peel.'

distinctions.note: Skin is a general word and for people or animals; peel refers to removing the outer layer of a fruit or vegetable.
Pare is more formal or old-fashioned for cutting away the outer skin, usually with a knife.

examples.everyday: Can you peel these carrots before dinner? I'm stuck on the sauce.
examples.professional: Our cafeteria peels the apples in the morning so the kitchen can slice them quickly.
examples.analytical: The poem peels back layers of appearance until only the bare fact remains.

nuance.analogy: Peeling is like taking off a jacket layer by layer until you reach the core.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'pelar,' from Latin 'pilare' (to remove hair).
common_mistakes: Confusing 'peel' (the skin) with 'peal' (a loud ringing sound), which is pronounced the same.
Using 'peel' for removing a person's skin in ordinary talk; it refers to foods or outer layers.

peel.etymology: From Middle English *pelen*, from Old English *pilian* and Old French *peler*, *pellier*; both from Latin *pilo* (“to remove hair, depilate”), from *pilus* (“hair”).

conversation.text: Can you peel the potatoes while I start the gravy?
Peel the shrimp before cooking, and keep the tails on.
I peeled an orange for my daughter.

senses.definition: Heavy, massive, weighty.
Serious, onerous, oppressive.
Clumsy, unwieldy, or slow, especially due to weight.
Dull, boring, tedious; long-winded in expression.
(rare) Characterized by or associated with pondering.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Very heavy, slow or clumsy, or too serious and dull in manner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PAHN. The second syllable is a rhotic er with little stress, and the ending -ous is pronounced us.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it usually suggests heaviness, slowness or dullness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ponderous mainly in writing or formal speech to criticize something as heavy or slow, such as a ponderous report or a ponderous machine. In casual talk people more often say clunky or long-winded. Using it for a person's humor or speech can sound sharp, so use it with care.

distinctions.note: Heavy describes physical weight, while ponderous can describe weight as well as slowness, dullness or excessive seriousness.
Clumsy describes awkward movement or handling, while ponderous emphasizes slow, heavy movement or style.

examples.everyday: The old truck was so ponderous on the hill that we had to go back down and try again.
examples.professional: The approval process is ponderous, with five separate reviews before any change goes live.
examples.analytical: Critics often describe Hegel's prose as ponderous, but its difficulty reflects a deliberate effort to hold complex ideas together.

nuance.analogy: A ponderous argument is like a heavy cart pulled by an old horse: it moves, but very slowly and with great effort.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ponderosus, heavy, from pondus, weight.
common_mistakes: Confusing ponderous with ponder, which is the verb for thinking deeply.
Pronouncing the final syllable as -us in a way that sounds like ponder-ous with extra stress.

senses.definition: A rectangular piece of thick paper or thin cardboard, typically used for sending messages by mail without the need for an envelope.
To send a postcard to someone.
senses.example: to postcard one's friends

senses.definition: To send by means of a postcard.
senses.example: to postcard one's news

core.definition: A card, usually with a picture on one side, that you write on and mail without an envelope, often sent by travelers.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on POHST, and the second syllable is lighter. The 'r' is pronounced strongly, and the 'o' in 'card' is the cot vowel of American English.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Postcards suggest friendly contact, vacations, and thinking of someone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans send postcards from vacations, often with a stamp and a short message, and people say 'I sent you a postcard'. The card does not need an envelope, unlike a greeting card. Postcards are common in tourist shops and national park gift stores.

distinctions.note: A greeting card is usually folded and sent in an envelope for a specific occasion; a postcard is flat and sent open for quick messages.
A letter is longer and more personal; a postcard is short and often has a photo on one side.

examples.everyday: We bought a postcard at the gift shop in Yellowstone and mailed it to my mom.
examples.professional: The marketing team mailed a postcard to our customers announcing the new store location.
examples.analytical: A postcard functions as a public form of private correspondence, since anyone handling it can read the message.

nuance.analogy: A postcard is like a short, open note on display: anyone handling it can read what you wrote.
nuance.etymology: Post from Latin positus, 'placed'; card from Greek khartes, 'papyrus leaf'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'postcard' with the stress on the second syllable.
Thinking you need an envelope for a postcard, which is not usual.

conversation.text: I sent my grandma a postcard from the Grand Canyon.
The view looked just like a postcard.
Do they sell postcards at the gift shop?

senses.definition: Of or relating to the showing or giving of preference.
senses.example: Club members received preferential seating.

senses.definition: Of or relating to a voting system in which the voters are allowed to indicate on their ballots their preference (usually their first and second choices) between two or more candidates, so that if no candidate receives a majority of first choices the one receiving the greatest number of first and second choices together is the winner.
senses.example: preferential voting; the preferential system

core.definition: Giving one person, group or option special advantage or favor over others, or relating to a ranked-choice voting method.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on EN, the third syllable. Keep the 'er' in the middle reduced, and make the ending 'shul' rather than 'shee-ul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical contexts, but it can sound unfair or exclusionary when used of special treatment for a group.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use preferential mainly in formal, legal, policy or voting contexts, such as 'preferential treatment' or 'preferential voting'. Preferential treatment in American debate can be controversial, so be precise about what you mean. In everyday conversation people usually say 'special treatment' or 'favored'.

distinctions.note: Preferred describes what is chosen or favored by someone; preferential describes the act of giving an advantage or the system that does so.
Favorable is broad and general; preferential specifically refers to being given priority or an advantage over others.

examples.everyday: My bank gives long-time customers a preferential rate on loans, which is nice when you're buying a house.
examples.professional: The vendor offered our team preferential access to the beta, so we can test the new features first.
examples.analytical: Preferential voting allows an election to reflect voters' full rankings, rather than only their first choice.

nuance.analogy: Preferential treatment is like a line that moves faster for certain guests, letting some people go ahead of others.
nuance.etymology: From preference, from Latin praeferre 'to carry before, to prefer'.
common_mistakes: Using preferential as a noun; the noun is preference, and preferential describes an advantage or system.
Saying 'preferencial' with an extra syllable; the word has five syllables and the stress is on EN.

senses.definition: Having greater or the greatest weight, quantity, importance or force.
senses.example: The judge gave preponderant weight to the physical evidence.

core.definition: Greater in weight, number, importance, or influence than other things in a group; dominant.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on POND, the second syllable. The unstressed endings reduce to weak vowels, so the last two syllables sound like -ruhnt, not -rant.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes dominance in a neutral, analytical way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in formal, academic, or legal writing. In everyday speech they would say most, main, or biggest. You can say a preponderant share, a preponderant influence, or a preponderant view.

distinctions.note: Dominant is common and can describe power or control, while preponderant is more formal and emphasizes greater weight or number.
Predominant and preponderant are close in meaning, but predominant more often describes prominence or visibility, and preponderant more often describes quantity or weight.

examples.everyday: Pasta is the preponderant choice at this family restaurant, so the menu is mostly noodles.
examples.professional: Our preponderant user base is on mobile, so the redesign should start with the phone layout.
examples.analytical: Locke gives preponderant weight to experience in shaping human knowledge, though he never fully excludes innate reasoning.

nuance.analogy: A preponderant factor is like the heavy weight on a scale that decides which side goes down.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praeponderare, to outweigh, from prae- before plus ponderare, to weigh.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as PRE-pon-der-ant.
Confusing it with predominant, which is close in meaning but usually refers to prominence rather than numbers.

preponderant.etymology: From Latin *praeponderāns*, present participle of *praeponderō* (“to outweigh”).

senses.definition: In a presumptuous manner; arrogantly.

core.definition: In a way that shows too much confidence or boldness, going beyond what is appropriate or permitted.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ZUMP. The syllables 'choo-us-lee' are weak, so the word has three unstressed syllables after the main stress. Keep the middle vowel reduced to a quick 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes someone for overstepping.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'presumptuously' in everyday talk. It appears mainly in formal writing, sermons and literary prose. In speech, people usually say 'it was presumptuous of him' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Boldly' can be admiring; 'presumptuously' is critical, implying the act went too far.
'Arrogantly' focuses on attitude; 'presumptuously' focuses on overstepping a boundary.

examples.everyday: He presumptuously opened my mail, and I was annoyed.
examples.professional: The consultant presumptuously rewrote our entire roadmap without asking the team.
examples.analytical: The author presumptuously claims to speak for the whole tradition in a single chapter.

nuance.analogy: Acting presumptuously is like reaching for the last slice of cake before anyone has offered it to you.
nuance.etymology: Formed from presumptuous and the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'presumptuously' in casual speech where 'presumptuous' as an adjective is more natural.
Mispronouncing the final syllable as 'chew-us-lee' with a stress shift.

senses.definition: A relational mental state connecting a person to a proposition, such as believing that, desiring that, or hoping that.

core.definition: A mental state, such as believing, hoping or desiring, that relates a person to a proposition.

pronunciation.tip: Both words have stress on a single main syllable, -ZI- in the first and AT- in the second. The -al in the first word is a light, reduced syllable, so say it quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical term from philosophy of mind and language.
nuance.usage_note: This is a specialist term used in philosophy of mind, epistemology and semantics. Americans would not use it in casual conversation. In plain speech they would say 'what someone believes, hopes or wants'.

distinctions.note: In ordinary English an 'attitude' is an emotional stance or manner, while in philosophy a propositional attitude is a relation between a mind and a proposition.

examples.everyday: When my roommate said she hoped it would not rain, a philosopher friend called that a propositional attitude.
examples.professional: In the model, each agent holds beliefs and desires as propositional attitudes toward the statements it encodes.
examples.analytical: Many philosophers hold that intentionality is best explained by propositional attitudes, such as believing that p or desiring that q.

nuance.analogy: A propositional attitude is like a sealed envelope: the mind holds it, and the content inside is the proposition.
nuance.etymology: Propositional comes from Latin propositio, 'a proposition'; attitude comes from Italian attitudine, 'posture'.
common_mistakes: Using 'attitude' in its everyday sense of mood or behavior.
Forgetting that the second word is stressed on the first syllable, AT-ih-tood.

senses.definition: The belief that all events are predetermined by God or fate.

core.definition: The belief that all events are predetermined and directed by God, fate or a higher power.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on DEN, with secondary stress on PRAH. The 'ti' sounds like 'sh', and the final '-ism' is a reduced 'iz-uhm'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in scholarly use; it can be critical when used to describe a view that minimizes human agency.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use providentialism mainly in historical, theological and academic writing, such as discussions of Puritan or American historical thought. In everyday speech it would sound very technical. People usually say 'belief in providence' or 'God's plan' instead.

distinctions.note: Providence is God's actual governance; providentialism is the belief or doctrine that everything happens by providence.
Fatalism says events are fixed regardless of divine purpose; providentialism ties predetermination to a purposeful God.

examples.everyday: My history professor says some Americans think about the nation's success as a kind of providentialism.
examples.professional: Our research summary avoids providentialism and explains outcomes through measured causes instead.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that providentialism shaped early American historiography by reading every catastrophe as a sign of divine judgment.

nuance.analogy: Like a script already written for a play: every scene is set, though the actors still perform it.
nuance.etymology: From providential plus the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Using it as a synonym for providence; providentialism is the belief system, not God's governance itself.
Stressing the wrong syllable; the main stress is on DEN.

senses.definition: To rove over, through, or about in a stealthy manner; especially, to search in, as for prey or booty.
senses.example: Watch the lioness prowling in the shrubbery for zebras.

senses.definition: To idle; to go about aimlessly.
senses.example: That dandy has nothing better to do than prowl around town all day in his pinstripe suit.

senses.definition: The act of prowling.
senses.example: I'm going on a midnight prowl.

core.definition: To move quietly and stealthily around an area, especially while looking for prey, an opportunity or something to steal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the single syllable PROWL, which rhymes with owl. The r is pronounced clearly, and the l at the end is a dark American l.

nuance.connotation: Negative or suspicious. It suggests sneaking around with bad intentions, though it can describe animals neutrally.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use prowl for animals hunting, and for people who are sneaking around, often with suspicious intentions, such as prowling around a parking lot. It is common in news and crime reporting. In casual talk people might say sneaking around or hanging around. Calling a person a prowler in a neighborhood can sound alarming.

distinctions.note: Sneak focuses on moving secretly to avoid being noticed, while prowl emphasizes searching or wandering in an area.
Roam means to wander freely with no clear goal, while prowl implies a purposeful, watchful search.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor's cat prowls around the backyard every evening looking for birds.
examples.professional: Security reviewed the footage and saw someone prowling around the loading dock after midnight.
examples.analytical: In the parable, the adversary is pictured as one who prowls, watching for the moment when the believer is least watchful.

nuance.analogy: To prowl is like a cat slowly circling a mouse hole: patient, quiet and always watching for the right moment.
nuance.etymology: Probably from Middle English prollen, to search or wander about, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Using prowl as a noun with the wrong stress or form; the noun is the same word, as in on the prowl.
Confusing prowl with prowler when describing a person; prowler is the person doing it.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word peripatei (περιπατεῖ), meaning walks about or moves around, underlies the RSV image of the adversary prowling. In 1 Peter 5:8 the devil is described as prowling like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour, which warns believers to be alert. Job 1:7 describes Satan going to and fro on the earth and walking up and down on it, a picture of restless searching that is close to the idea of prowling.

prowl.etymology: From Middle English *prollen*, of unknown origin.

senses.definition: An expert in a particular field, especially as called upon to provide comment or opinion in the media; a commentator, a critic.
A learned person in India; someone with knowledge of Sanskrit, philosophy, religion and law; a Hindu scholar.
(historical) A native surveyor in British India, trained to carry out clandestine surveillance beyond British borders.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: An expert who comments publicly on news and current events, especially on television or in the media.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PUN. The second syllable is a short, reduced vowel, so say it as a quick dit rather than DEET.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It can praise a respected expert, but it often suggests someone who talks too confidently about topics in the media.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pundit mostly for political and economic commentators on cable news, talk shows and opinion columns. Calling someone a pundit is often mildly critical, implying they speak loudly without deep proof. The original Indian sense of a learned scholar is rare in American speech.

distinctions.note: An expert has real specialized knowledge; a pundit is known mainly for offering opinions in public media.
Commentator is neutral and describes the role; pundit adds a sense of frequent, often confident, prediction.

examples.everyday: My brother quotes every political pundit on TV, but he never checks their predictions.
examples.professional: The marketing team should not treat every industry pundit's prediction as a reliable forecast.
examples.analytical: Public discourse now rewards the pundit who speaks with certainty, even when the evidence is weak.

nuance.analogy: A pundit is like a weather forecaster who is always on screen, sometimes right, and rarely held to account.
nuance.etymology: From Hindi pandit, a learned man, from Sanskrit pandita, learned.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as a long vowel, as in DEET.
Using pundit to mean a respected scholar in ordinary American English.

pundit.etymology: Borrowed from *पंडित* / *پنڈت*, from Sanskrit *पण्डित* (“scholar, learned man, teacher, philosopher”).

senses.definition: To put (something) in its usual storage place; to place out of the way, clean up.
senses.example: Please put away the tools when you are finished.

senses.definition: To store, add to one's stores for later use.
senses.example: putting a little away for a rainy day

senses.definition: To consume (food or drink), especially in large quantities.
senses.example: You wouldn't think such a small person could put away so much food.

senses.definition: To send (someone) to prison or mental asylum.
senses.example: After he was convicted, they put him away for 10 years.

senses.definition: To kill someone.
To discard, divest oneself of.
To hit the ball in such a way that the opponent cannot reach it; see passing shot.
To knock out an opponent.
senses.example: He put away his opponent in the first round.

senses.definition: To take a large lead in a game, especially enough to guarantee victory or make the game no longer competitive.
senses.example: They put the game away by scoring three touchdowns in the fourth quarter.

senses.definition: To strike out a batter.
To catch a fly ball or tag out a baserunner.

core.definition: To return something to its usual storage place, or to tidy and store items out of sight after using them.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'way', and 'put' is quick and light. Americans reduce 'away' to 'uh-WAY', so do not say 'uh-WAH' with a separate, heavy vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a practical, everyday instruction about tidying up.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'Put the dishes away' or 'Put your toys away' at home, and 'put away' is very common in everyday speech. For eating, it is informal and can imply someone ate a lot, as in 'He put away three tacos'. In storage or savings contexts it means setting money aside.

distinctions.note: Put back means return something to where it was; put away means store it in a proper, usually out-of-sight place.
Clean up is broader and can include wiping or sweeping; put away focuses on storing items in their proper place.

examples.everyday: Could you put away the groceries before the ice cream melts?
examples.professional: Please put away your laptops and notes before we start the review so the room is clear for the presentation.
examples.analytical: The chapter describes how the household learned to put away its goods carefully, linking domestic order with a moral discipline of care.

nuance.analogy: Putting something away is like filing a document back in its folder so you can find it again later.
common_mistakes: Placing the object after 'away' with a pronoun; say 'put it away', not 'put away it'.
Using 'put away' for 'put on', which means to dress or add clothing.

conversation.text: Put your toys away before bed, please.
I put away the groceries while you were out.
We try to put away a little every month for college.
He can really put away the pizza.
Can you help me put away the groceries?
I washed the dishes, but I didn't put them away.

senses.definition: To postpone, especially through procrastination.
senses.example: Don't put off your homework to the last minute.

senses.definition: To cause to dislike; to discourage (from doing).
senses.example: Almost drowning put him off swimming.

senses.definition: To delay (a task, event, etc.).
senses.example: The storm put off the game by a week.

senses.definition: To distract; to disturb the concentration of.
senses.example: Please be quiet. I'm trying to concentrate and you're putting me off.

senses.definition: To emit; to give off (an odor, smoke, etc.).
senses.example: This type of firewood puts off a strong smell.

senses.definition: Offended, repulsed.
senses.example: The guest was quite put off by an odor.

senses.definition: Daunted or fazed.
senses.example: All but the most dedicated were put off by the huge task.

core.definition: To postpone something, or to make someone dislike or be discouraged from doing something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on OFF, and the vowel is the same in cot and caught for many Americans, so it may sound like 'ahf'. Keep the f clear and do not add a t sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative when it means delaying something you should do, or discouraging someone; neutral when it means rescheduling a meeting.
nuance.usage_note: In meetings, Americans say 'Can we put off this decision until next week?' to postpone politely. As an adjective, 'put off' means offended or repelled, and it is often used with 'by'. Using it for procrastination on personal tasks can sound like a mild criticism, so it fits casual talk well.

distinctions.note: 'Postpone' is more formal and neutral, often used in writing and official notices, while 'put off' is more casual and spoken.
'Delay' suggests something unexpected causing lateness, while 'put off' usually implies a deliberate choice to wait.
'Discourage' focuses on reducing someone's motivation, while 'put off' in this sense often means turning someone away with an unpleasant feeling.

collocations: be put off by the price

examples.everyday: I keep putting off calling the dentist, but I really should do it today.
examples.professional: Can we put off the sprint review until the new data pipeline is stable?
examples.analytical: Augustine warned that people who put off repentance tend to find the decision harder with each passing year.

nuance.analogy: Like sliding a heavy box to the back of a closet so you do not have to deal with it yet.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'put off' with 'put on' when describing something you dislike.
Using 'put off' with a person as object without 'by' in the discouraging sense; say 'I was put off by the rude staff'.

conversation.text: Stop putting off your homework and just do it.
We put the meeting off until next Tuesday.
The smell of the place really put me off.
Let's put off the decision until next week.
I keep putting off my expense report.
Some customers were put off by the high price.

senses.definition: The quality or state of being radiant; shining, bright or splendid.
The flux of radiation emitted per unit solid angle in a given direction by a unit area of a source.

core.definition: A warm, bright glow of light, or a visible happiness and joy that seems to shine from someone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the last two syllables as one quick sound, 'ens'. Do not add an extra syllable between 'di' and 'ens'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes beauty, warmth and joy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use radiance for light or for a person's glowing happiness, often in writing, speeches, and descriptions of weddings or happy moments. In casual talk people more often say 'she was glowing' or 'she looked so happy'. It sounds warm rather than dramatic.

distinctions.note: Brightness describes how much light there is, while radiance adds a warm, glowing quality that seems to come from within.

examples.everyday: She had a radiance about her after the baby was born, and everybody noticed.
examples.professional: The new brand guide wants a warm radiance in our product photos, not a harsh flash.
examples.analytical: Augustine describes the soul's radiance as a reflection of a light that comes from beyond it.

nuance.analogy: Radiance is like the glow of a lamp through a paper shade, warm and soft rather than harsh.
nuance.etymology: From Latin radiare, 'to shine', from radius, 'ray'.
common_mistakes: Using radiance for ordinary light, where 'brightness' is more natural.
Confusing radiance with radiation, which is a technical term for energy emitted in waves or particles.

senses.definition: A line segment between any point of a circle or sphere and its center.
senses.example: Fatima claims to have visited all the bars within a five-mile radius of her Manhattan apartment.

senses.definition: The length of this line segment.
The minimum eccentricity of any vertex, for a given graph.
Anything resembling a radius, such as the spoke of a wheel, the movable arm of a sextant, or one of the radiating lines of a spider's web.
The long bone in the forearm, on the side of the thumb.
The lighter bone (or fused portion of bone) in the forelimb of an animal.
One of the major veins of the insect wing, between the subcosta and the media; the vein running along the costal edge of the discal cell.
To give a rounded edge to.

core.definition: A straight line from the center of a circle or sphere to its edge, or the length of that line.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the last syllable as a reduced 'us' rather than 'ass'. The middle 'di' is a quick 'dee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise mathematical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use radius in math, geometry, and everyday talk about distance, as in 'within a five-mile radius'. The plural is radii, pronounced RAY-dee-eye. In casual speech, people often say 'a circle within this radius' when describing a distance from a point.

distinctions.note: Diameter is the full width of a circle through its center, which is twice the radius.

examples.everyday: Every restaurant within a ten-mile radius of our house has a waiting list this weekend.
examples.professional: The model only works if we set the search radius to five kilometers around each store.
examples.analytical: Euclid defines the circle by the constant radius that joins every point on its edge to the center.

nuance.analogy: A radius is like a spoke of a bicycle wheel, running from the hub to the rim.
nuance.etymology: From Latin radius, 'ray, spoke of a wheel, staff'.
common_mistakes: Using the singular radius for more than one line; the plural is radii.
Confusing radius with diameter, which is twice as long.

senses.definition: An otherworldly dimension or domain — magical, ethereal, or otherwise.
A sphere of knowledge or of influence; a domain.
senses.example: the realm of physics

senses.definition: A taxonomic rank in the phylogeny of viruses, higher than kingdoms.
A grouping of equally trusted computers managed together on a network.
A primary zoogeographical division of the earth's surface.

core.definition: A kingdom, or more broadly any area or field of activity, thought or existence.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable, with the l pronounced but a silent-sounding ending that blends into the m. Do not add a vowel like 'relum' or 'real-um.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly elevated. It sounds grand or literary in everyday contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use realm in formal, literary and fantasy contexts, such as 'the realm of possibility' or 'the realm of science.' In casual talk people more often say 'area,' 'field' or 'world.' A casual reply to something in your field is usually 'Oh, that's your area,' not a comment on realms.

distinctions.note: Domain is more technical and common in computing and science; realm sounds more literary and broad.
Field is the everyday word for a branch of study or work; realm sounds more grand.

examples.everyday: That kind of mistake is outside the realm of my experience, honestly.
examples.professional: This question falls within the realm of the data platform team, not the product team.
examples.analytical: The author argues that moral obligation extends beyond the realm of human agents to the natural world.

nuance.analogy: A realm is like a country on a map: it has borders and its own rules, but it sits inside a bigger world.
nuance.etymology: From Old French reaume, from Latin regimen, 'rule.'
common_mistakes: Adding an extra vowel sound at the end, such as 'relum.'
Using realm for a simple room or location; it names an abstract or grand domain.

realm.etymology: From Middle English *rewme*, *realme*, *reaume*, from Old French *reaume*, *realme*, *reialme* (“kingdom”), of unclear origins.

senses.definition: To cut (for example a grain) with a sickle, scythe, or reaping machine.
To gather (e.g. a harvest) by cutting.
To obtain or receive as a reward, in a good or a bad sense.
senses.example: to reap a benefit from exertions

senses.definition: To terminate a child process that has previously exited, thereby removing it from the process table.
senses.example: Until a child process is reaped, it may be listed in the process table as a zombie or defunct process.

senses.definition: To rape.
A bundle of grain; a handful of grain laid down by the reaper as it is cut.

core.definition: To cut and gather a crop at harvest, or to receive what you earned from earlier actions.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable, with a long e and a final p. Do not add a y sound or a voiced b at the end, which would make it sound like 'reeb.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in farming contexts; positive when used for rewards and negative when used for consequences.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reap most often in the figurative phrase 'you reap what you sow' to mean that actions bring consequences. Farming use is common in rural areas and in writing about agriculture. A natural reply to the proverb is 'Yeah, that's true,' or 'I guess I'm paying for it now.'

distinctions.note: Harvest is the general word for gathering crops; reap focuses on the cutting action, and it is also used figuratively.
Gain is a neutral word for getting something; reap implies receiving something as a result of earlier effort or action.

examples.everyday: After months of training, she's finally reaping the rewards of all that hard work.
examples.professional: If we invest in better documentation now, we'll reap the benefits when new engineers join.
examples.analytical: Paul's principle that a man reaps what he sows presents moral causality as a pattern built into human life.

nuance.analogy: Like a gardener who plants seeds in spring and gathers the crop in fall: what you put in is what comes back.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ripan, 'to seize, reap.'
common_mistakes: Confusing reap with reep as spelled, or with the word reed, which is a plant.
Using reap in the sense of getting something you did not earn, without implying a connection to earlier action.
nuance.biblical_note: Greek therizō (to reap, harvest) and therismos (harvest) appear in the New Testament. In Galatians 6:7-8 reaping is a metaphor for the consequences of sowing good or bad actions. In Matthew 13:30 the wheat is gathered into the barn at harvest, a picture of the final judgment in the parable of the wheat and tares.

reap.etymology: From Middle English *repen*, from Old English *rēopan*, *rēpan*, variants of, from **rīpan*, from Proto-Germanic **rīpaną*, from Proto-Indo-European **h₁reyb-* (“to snatch”).

senses.definition: Mental or spiritual refreshment.
Physical refreshment, especially with food or drink.
A meal, especially a light meal.

core.definition: A light meal or refreshment, or a restoring of the mind or spirit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, FEK. The final -tion is pronounced 'shun', and the first syllable is a weak 'rih'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests a restful, restorative pause, often with a simple meal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use refection in everyday talk. It appears in formal, religious, or old-fashioned writing, such as monastic or academic contexts. In normal conversation, people say a snack, a light lunch, or a break instead.

distinctions.note: Refreshment is the common everyday word for food or drink; refection is more formal and suggests a restorative meal.
Refectory is the dining hall of a monastery or school; refection is the meal or act of refreshment itself.

examples.everyday: After the long hike we took a short refection at the picnic table, just some bread and fruit.
examples.professional: The retreat schedule includes a light refection after the morning session, so participants can rest before the workshop.
examples.analytical: Scripture reading and prayer are offered as a spiritual refection, restoring the soul as food restores the body.

nuance.analogy: A refection is like a cup of tea after a long meeting: small, restorative, and meant to set you right again.
nuance.etymology: From Latin reficere, 'to make again, restore'.
common_mistakes: Confusing refection with reflection, which means thinking or a mirror image.
Using refection as a common everyday word for lunch; it sounds formal or archaic.

refection.etymology: From French *réfection*, from Latin *refectiōnem*, accusative singular of *refectiō* (“recovery, refection”), from *reficiō* (“restore, renew”).

senses.definition: To purify; reduce to a fine, unmixed, or pure state; to free from impurities.
senses.example: to refine gold

senses.definition: To become pure; to be cleared of impure matter.
To purify of coarseness, vulgarity, inelegance, etc. to polish.
senses.example: to refine someone's manners

senses.definition: To improve in accuracy, delicacy, or excellence.
To make nice or subtle.
senses.example: to refine thought

core.definition: To improve something by removing impurities or by making it more precise, polished or better developed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, fine. The first syllable is a reduced vowel, so do not say REE-fine.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It implies improvement and care.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use refine in business, engineering and everyday talk about improving ideas or skills. In a workplace, you might say 'Let's refine the proposal' or 'We need to refine the process.' It is more formal than 'improve' and sounds thoughtful rather than stiff.

distinctions.note: Improve is general and everyday, while refine suggests careful, detailed adjustments to something that already works.
Polish focuses on surface finish or a final touch, while refine can involve deeper changes to a plan, process or product.

examples.everyday: I'm going to refine my cooking skills this summer by taking a class.
examples.professional: Let's refine the forecast model before we present it to the executive team on Thursday.
examples.analytical: A philosophical argument must be refined through repeated testing against counterexamples.

nuance.analogy: Refining is like panning for gold: you wash away the dirt and keep only the pure metal.
nuance.etymology: From re- and fine, from Latin finire, to end, and later to make fine or pure.
common_mistakes: Using refine with a direct object that is a person, as in 'refine him', which is unnatural.
Confusing refine with define in technical writing.

senses.definition: Of a relation R on a set S, such that xRx for all members x of S (that is, the relation holds between any element of the set and itself).
senses.example: "Equals" is a reflexive relation, as it holds for all possible x; "not less" is non-reflexive because it is true only for some x and y, "unequal" is irreflexive, as it never holds between x and itself.

senses.definition: Referring back to the subject, or having an object equal to the subject.
Of or resulting from a reflex.
senses.example: The electric shock elicited an automatic and reflexive response from him.

senses.definition: Producing immediate response, spontaneous.
senses.example: a reflexive dislike

senses.definition: Producing or provoking a reciprocal response.
Synonym of reflective.
A reflexive pronoun.
A reflexive verb.

core.definition: In mathematics, describing a relation R on a set S where every element x satisfies xRx, so the relation holds between each element and itself.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, FLEK. Reduce the final -ive to a short, weak 'iv' sound, and keep the first vowel reduced to 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In American math courses, 'reflexive' is standard vocabulary for relations, alongside symmetric and transitive. Outside math, Americans use the adjective for grammar, as in 'reflexive pronoun', and rarely use it in everyday speech. In the sense of a quick physical response, Americans say 'reflex' or 'automatic'.

distinctions.note: A symmetric relation means that if xRy then yRx; a reflexive relation means every element is related to itself. A relation can be one, both, or neither.
Transitive concerns chaining: if xRy and yRz then xRz. It is a separate property from reflexivity.

examples.everyday: My grammar app keeps flagging 'himself' as a reflexive pronoun, and I never remember why.
examples.professional: Before we merge the two tables, we should verify that the join key relation is reflexive and symmetric.
examples.analytical: A relation on a set is reflexive when every element stands in that relation to itself, and this property is independent of symmetry and transitivity.

nuance.analogy: A reflexive relation is like a mirror: every element looks back at itself.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin reflexivus, from reflexus, past participle of reflectere, to bend back.
common_mistakes: Saying 'reflective' for the mathematical sense; reflective means thoughtful or reflecting light.
Stressing the second syllable of 'reflexive' incorrectly as 'ruh-FLEX-iv' with a long vowel.

reflexive.etymology: From Medieval Latin *reflexīvus*, from Latin *reflexus*, equivalent to *reflex* + *-ive*.

senses.definition: Corrected; amended; restored to purity or excellence; said, specifically, of the whole body of Protestant churches originating in the Reformation, or, in a more restricted sense, of those who separated from Martin Luther on the doctrine of consubstantiation, etc. and carried the Reformation, as they claimed, to a higher point.
Amended in character and life.
senses.example: a reformed gambler/drunkard/alcoholic/criminal

core.definition: Corrected or improved in character or behavior; in religion, describing Protestant churches following the teaching of Calvin or Zwingli.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'FORM'. The final -ed is silent here, so the word ends in a 'md' sound; many learners add an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive for people who have changed their behavior; neutral or technical in religious contexts.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, 'reformed' describes someone who has changed their bad habits, as in 'a reformed smoker'. In theology, capital R 'Reformed' names a specific Protestant tradition, the Presbyterian and Calvinist churches. Context usually makes the meaning clear.

distinctions.note: Repentant stresses sorrow for wrongdoing, while reformed stresses the visible change in conduct afterward.
Rehabilitated is more formal and often used for people recovering from addiction or prison, while reformed is broader.

examples.everyday: My brother is a reformed night owl now and goes to bed before eleven.
examples.professional: The team lead is a reformed micromanager who now trusts the engineers to make their own calls.
examples.analytical: The Reformed tradition emphasizes God's sovereignty in salvation, which distinguishes it from other Protestant emphases.

nuance.analogy: A reformed habit is like a repaired road: it still works, but you can see where it was fixed.
nuance.etymology: From reform, from Latin reformare, to form again.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -ed as a separate syllable.
Confusing capital 'Reformed' (a church tradition) with a lowercase description of someone's character.

senses.definition: The act of moving from one place to another.
Renewal of a lease.
The assigning of addresses to variables either at linkage editing, or at runtime.

core.definition: The act of moving a person, business, or operation from one place to another, usually to live or work there.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on KAY, with a lighter secondary stress on the first syllable. The middle syllables are weak; the final -tion is pronounced shun, not tee-on.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a formal, professional way to talk about moving, often in workplace or government contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use relocation most often for an employer moving staff, a company moving offices, or a government moving families. In casual speech, people say moving or we're moving. The word can sound stiff in a personal conversation, so save it for work and official settings.

distinctions.note: Move is everyday and general. Relocation is formal and usually implies a planned, longer-term change of home or base.
Migration often refers to large groups or seasonal movement across regions or countries. Relocation usually describes an individual, family or company moving.
Transfer means moving to a different office or unit within the same organization. Relocation emphasizes the change of location itself.

examples.everyday: We're still recovering from the stress of our relocation to Austin last spring.
examples.professional: The company offers a generous relocation package for engineers who accept positions at the Seattle office.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the relocation of the capital reflected political strategy or simply practical concerns about defense.

nuance.analogy: Relocation is like transplanting a plant: the whole root system must move, not just the leaves.
nuance.etymology: From re- 'again' plus locate, from Latin locare, 'to place', with the sense 'to place again in a new location'.
common_mistakes: Using relocation for a short trip or visit; it implies moving for a longer stay.
Using the preposition 'in' or 'at' incorrectly; say relocation to a city.
Stressing the wrong syllable; the stress falls on KAY.

senses.definition: Turned up, especially when describing the nose.

core.definition: Turned upward at the tip, used especially for a nose that is slightly upturned.

pronunciation.tip: This is a French word, so the final syllable is stressed and sounds like 'say'. The middle vowel is a long 'oo'. Do not pronounce the final e separately.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a feature, often in a flattering way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in conversation. It appears in fashion, art, descriptions of people in novels, and cosmetic writing. In everyday speech people say 'upturned nose' or 'turned-up nose'.

distinctions.note: Upturned is the everyday English word; retroussé is a more literary French loanword for a nose or similar feature.
A snub nose is short and turned up; retroussé describes the upturn itself, without implying the nose is short.

examples.everyday: My grandmother always said I had a little retroussé nose, just like hers.
examples.professional: In the fashion sketch, the designer drew the collar with a retroussé edge to give it a playful look.
examples.analytical: The novelist uses the retroussé nose as a marker of youthful charm, contrasting it with the sharp profiles of the older characters.

nuance.analogy: A retroussé nose is like a little ski tip turned up at the front.
nuance.etymology: From French retrousser, to turn up, from re- and trousser, to tuck up.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'SAY-kay' or dropping it.
Using it as a noun, when it is an adjective.

retroussé.etymology: From French *retroussé*, past participle of *retrousser* (“to hitch up, hike up”), from *re-* (from Latin *re-* (“back, backwards; again”), from Proto-Italic **wre-* (“again”)) + *trousser* (“to fold up, hitch up”).

senses.definition: An expert or student of rhetoric.
senses.example: Themistocles was a rhetorician.

senses.definition: An orator or eloquent public speaker.

core.definition: A person who is an expert in rhetoric, or a skilled and eloquent public speaker.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on RISH, the third syllable, and the first syllable has a lighter stress. The t is a flap, so it sounds like 'reh-duh-RISH-un', and the final -ian is reduced to 'un'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rhetorician mostly in academic writing about classical rhetoric or in literary criticism. It can be slightly complimentary when describing a skilled speaker, but it sounds formal and old-fashioned in ordinary talk. People more often say 'speaker', 'orator', or 'expert in persuasion'.

distinctions.note: An orator is a speaker, often formal or ceremonial, while a rhetorician may be a scholar of persuasion or a skilled theorist.
A sophist uses clever argument for money or victory, often with a negative tone, while a rhetorician can be a serious teacher of the art.

examples.everyday: My grandfather was a rhetorician at heart; every story he told was built to make you laugh and then agree with him.
examples.professional: The department hired a rhetorician to help the engineers present their findings to nontechnical executives.
examples.analytical: Quintilian presents himself as a rhetorician who trains the ideal orator, and his treatise links moral character with persuasive skill.

nuance.analogy: Like a chess coach: the rhetorician knows the moves of persuasion and can teach them, even if they do not always play the game in public.
nuance.etymology: From Greek rhētōr, orator, through Latin rhetor, with the suffix -ician.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the first syllable as 'REH-tuh-ri-shun'; the stress is on RISH.
Confusing rhetorician with 'rhetoric', which is the art itself rather than a person.

rhetorician.etymology: From Middle English *rethoricien*, from Old French *retoricien*; equivalent to *rhetoric* + *-ian*.

senses.definition: In AI: Recurrent neural network: a network that processes sequences step by step, carrying a hidden state from one step to the next.
Initialism of random neural network.
Initialism of recurrent neural network.
Initialism of recursive neural network.

core.definition: Recurrent neural network: a neural network that processes sequences one step at a time, carrying a hidden state forward.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters separately: ar, en, EN, with the main stress on the final letter. It is never pronounced as one word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise term in machine learning and signal processing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans in AI, data science, and engineering say the letters individually. In AI, RNN means recurrent neural network, not random neural network, which is rare. Modern teams often use transformers instead, so mention of RNN usually comes up in historical or sequence-modeling discussions.

distinctions.note: A CNN, or convolutional neural network, is strong at spatial patterns such as images, while an RNN processes ordered sequences such as text or time series.
A transformer processes sequences in parallel with attention, while an RNN processes one step at a time with a hidden state.

examples.everyday: My coworker said his first chatbot project used an RNN before they switched to newer models.
examples.professional: We benchmarked the RNN against the transformer, and the transformer was faster on long sequences.
examples.analytical: The RNN's hidden state gives it a form of memory, but gradients can vanish across long sequences, which motivated gated architectures.

nuance.analogy: An RNN is like a reader who keeps a running summary in mind while reading one word at a time.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of recurrent neural network.
common_mistakes: Saying RNN as one word, like ren or ran.
Expanding RNN as random neural network; in AI, it means recurrent neural network.

conversation.text: The RNN reads the sensor readings in order and predicts the next value.
Transformers largely replaced the RNN for language tasks because they parallelize better during training.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to leaps or leaping.
Proceeding by leaps rather than by smooth, continuous variation.

core.definition: Moving or changing by sudden jumps or leaps rather than in smooth, gradual steps.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SAL, with a secondary stress on tor. The middle syllable is a weak uh, and the final syllable is a light ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise descriptive word used in science and formal writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use saltatory in everyday speech; it appears in biology, geology, economics, and literary descriptions of dance or sudden movement. In a professional setting it sounds precise and specialized, so explain it if your audience is not technical. Plain alternatives like 'sudden' or 'jumpy' are more natural in conversation.

distinctions.note: Sudden describes any abrupt event, while saltatory specifically describes change that proceeds in leaps rather than gradual steps.
Gradual is the opposite idea, describing slow, smooth change, which saltatory contrasts with.

examples.everyday: Our old phone's battery went from sixty percent to ten in a jerky, saltatory way.
examples.professional: The team's progress was saltatory, with big jumps after each release and long quiet stretches between.
examples.analytical: Some evolutionary theorists argue that species change in saltatory bursts rather than through smooth, continuous variation.

nuance.analogy: Saltatory change is like a staircase rather than a ramp: you move from one level to the next in jumps, not in a smooth slope.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'saltatorius', relating to dancing or leaping, from 'saltare', to leap or dance.
common_mistakes: Confusing saltatory with salutary, which means beneficial.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying sal-TAY-tory instead of SAL-tuh-tor-ee.

senses.definition: The sheath of a sword.
To put an object (especially a sword) into its scabbard.
senses.example: Suddenly he scabbarded his sabre.

core.definition: A protective sheath that holds a sword or long blade when it is not in use.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a weak, reduced 'erd', not a full 'ard'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive word for weapons and historical objects.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scabbard mostly for swords and historical or fantasy contexts, and in museums. For knives, people often say sheath, and for handguns they say holster.

distinctions.note: Sheath is the general word for any blade cover; scabbard is the specific term for a sword.
A holster is worn to carry a pistol, not a blade.

examples.everyday: The old sword in the museum still has its original scabbard.
examples.professional: The conservator recorded the wear on the leather scabbard before cleaning.
examples.analytical: The scabbard in the medieval image signifies restraint, the blade held back until the moment of judgment.

nuance.analogy: Like a case for a pair of scissors that keeps the blade safe until it is needed.
common_mistakes: Confusing scabbard with scab, which is a skin crust.
Using scabbard for a gun holder; the word is for swords.

scabbard.etymology: From Middle English *scabard*, *scauberde*, *scauberk*, *scauberke*, from Anglo-Norman *eschaubert*, *escalberc*, of origin, perhaps from **skarberg* (“sheath”), from Proto-Germanic **skēriz* (“blade, scissors”) + **bergaz* (“shelter, protection, refuge”).

senses.definition: The condition of something being scarce or deficient.
An inadequate amount of something; a shortage.
senses.example: a scarcity of grain

core.definition: A situation in which something is in short supply or there is not enough of it for everyone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, 'SKAIR', and make the final syllable a short, reduced 'tee'. The middle vowel is a quick 'ih' sound, not a full 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes a lack of something important and often implies a problem to be solved.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'scarcity' in news, economics, business and everyday talk about shortages, such as 'water scarcity' or 'a scarcity of housing'. It sounds more formal than 'shortage', and it often implies a long-term or structural problem rather than a temporary one.

distinctions.note: A 'shortage' is often temporary, such as a shortage of gas during a strike. 'Scarcity' often describes a deeper, ongoing lack of something.
'Lack' simply means not having something. 'Scarcity' implies that the thing is rare or hard to obtain.

examples.everyday: There's a real scarcity of good parking downtown, so get there early.
examples.professional: The data team faces a scarcity of labeled examples, which limits how well the model generalizes.
examples.analytical: Economists argue that scarcity forces societies to make choices about how to allocate limited resources.

nuance.analogy: Scarcity is like a bottle with only a few drops left: everyone wants some, but there is not enough to go around.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'escarcete', from 'escars', meaning scant or little.
common_mistakes: Using 'scarcity' for a short, temporary problem, when 'shortage' would be more natural.
Using 'scarcity' as a countable noun, as in 'a scarcity of many things'; it is usually uncountable.

senses.definition: Malicious enjoyment derived from observing someone else's misfortune; counterempathy.

core.definition: Pleasure you feel when someone else suffers a misfortune or failure, especially someone you envy or dislike.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SHAH. The second syllable is a reduced vowel, so say 'dun' rather than 'den' or 'dee', and end with a soft 'duh' rather than a strong 'dah'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a malicious or unkind pleasure, so it is used to criticize someone's attitude rather than as a compliment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in conversation or writing about gossip, office rivalries, celebrity news or politics. It is a borrowed German word, but people use it in ordinary speech, often with a slightly knowing or joking tone. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I know, it's hard not to feel a little schadenfreude,' which admits the feeling without sounding cruel.

distinctions.note: Gloating is the open, showy expression of satisfaction over someone's defeat, while schadenfreude is the private feeling itself.
Spite is a desire to hurt or annoy someone, whereas schadenfreude is simply enjoying their misfortune without necessarily causing it.

examples.everyday: When my neighbor's fantasy football team lost by a hundred points, I'll admit I felt a little schadenfreude.
examples.professional: Some people in the department felt schadenfreude when the rival team's product launch failed, but we should focus on our own roadmap.
examples.analytical: Schadenfreude reveals something about the moral psychology of comparison, since pleasure at another's suffering often depends on a prior sense of rivalry or inequality.

nuance.analogy: Schadenfreude is like a small sip of sweetness that comes from someone else's bitter moment, tasty to the taker but unkind to the one who tastes the bitterness.
nuance.etymology: From German Schaden (harm, damage) and Freude (joy).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as SHAD-en-FROID, with a French ending or a long 'ay' sound in the first syllable.
Using it as a neutral word for any happiness, when it always implies enjoying someone else's pain.

senses.definition: A mind-dependent object whose existence and properties are known directly to human beings in perception.

core.definition: In philosophy, the immediate, mind-dependent objects of perception, such as colors, sounds, or tastes, that we are directly aware of in experience.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DAY in American speech, while SENS gets a lighter secondary stress. Many Americans say DAT-uh in casual speech, but DAY-tuh is the standard academic pronunciation. Keep the final schwa light and do not say the second word as 'data' with an 'ah' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: This is a term of art used mainly in philosophy of perception, epistemology, and cognitive science. Philosophers use it in debates about whether we perceive physical objects directly or only through mind-dependent items. Outside those fields, Americans say 'what I see' or 'sensory information' instead.

distinctions.note: Sense data are the items we are actually aware of in perception, while sensibilia are things that could be sensed, whether or not anyone senses them.
Sensory information is a general, everyday term for what the senses gather, whereas sense data is a technical philosophical term for mind-dependent objects of awareness.

examples.everyday: My friend and I got into a long argument about whether we really see the table or only our sense data of it.
examples.professional: In the cognitive science seminar, the team reviewed how sense data models relate to raw camera input in the vision system.
examples.analytical: Berkeley's argument presupposes that sense data are the only immediate objects of perception, and this premise is what the realist must reject.

nuance.analogy: Like the frames of a film projected on a screen, sense data are what appear to the viewer, not the actual scene behind the projector.
nuance.etymology: Sense from Latin sensus 'feeling, perception'; datum from Latin datum 'something given'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'sense datas' as the plural; the plural is 'sense data', which takes a plural verb in academic use.
Stressing SENS-data equally, which makes the phrase sound flat; the main stress is on DAY.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being sentient; possession of consciousness or sensory awareness.

core.definition: The capacity to have subjective experiences, such as feeling pain, pleasure, or awareness of one's surroundings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SEN. The ending -ence is reduced to a short 'uns' sound, not the full 'ence' spelling.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise philosophical or scientific term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sentience mainly in philosophy, animal ethics, neuroscience, and discussions of artificial intelligence. It is rarely used in casual talk, where people say conscious or aware. In debates about AI, the word usually concerns whether a system can actually feel, not just process information.

distinctions.note: Consciousness is broader and includes thinking and self-awareness. Sentience is narrower and usually means the capacity to feel sensations or emotions.
Intelligence concerns problem-solving and reasoning ability. Sentience concerns having experiences, which may exist without high intelligence.

examples.everyday: My vet says there is good evidence of sentience in pigs, so they should be treated with care.
examples.professional: Before we ship the chatbot, legal wants a clear answer on whether we can claim any sentience in the model.
examples.analytical: Whether sentience requires embodiment is a live question, because a system can model pain without ever having anything it is like to feel it.

nuance.analogy: Sentience is the lights being on inside: something is experienced, not just processed.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sentire, to feel.
common_mistakes: Confusing sentience with sentiment, which refers to emotions or opinions.
Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable instead of the first.

sentience.etymology: From *sentient*, from Latin *sentiēns*, present participle of *sentiō* (“feel, sense”).

senses.definition: The state of being serene; calmness; peacefulness.
A lack of agitation or disturbance.
A title given to a reigning prince or similar dignitary.

core.definition: A state of calm and peacefulness, free from worry, agitation, or disturbance.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on REN, the second syllable. The final -ity is a reduced vowel that sounds like 'ih' followed by 'tee', so it is not 'ee-tee' with a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It names a calm state that people value and seek, such as inner peace or the calm of a place. It sounds slightly more elevated than calm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use serenity in conversation about a peaceful place, a quiet morning, or inner calm, and in writing about spirituality or wellness. In everyday speech calm or peace is more common. The word is also a formal title for princes, so context matters.

distinctions.note: Calm is everyday and general; serenity implies a deeper, more lasting peace.
Tranquility suggests quiet and stillness in a setting; serenity often describes the calm of a person or a view.
Composure is calm maintained under pressure; serenity can exist without any pressure at all.

examples.everyday: Sitting on the porch with a cup of coffee in the morning gives me a real sense of serenity.
examples.professional: Her serenity during the outage kept the whole incident bridge from panicking.
examples.analytical: For Augustine, the serenity of the soul comes only when the heart rests in God.

nuance.analogy: Serenity is like a clear mountain lake: even when the wind blows over the land, the deep water stays still.
nuance.etymology: From Latin serenitas, from serenus, meaning clear or calm.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable: 'sir-EN-ih-tee' is wrong; the stress is on the second syllable, 'suh-REN'.
Confusing it with the title 'Serene Highness', which is a formal address for a prince; in everyday speech it means calm.

serenity.etymology: From Middle English *serenyte*, from Old French *serenité*, from Latin *serēnitās*, equivalent to *serene* + *ity*.

senses.definition: To divide and distribute.
To give part of what one has to somebody else to use or consume.
To have or use in common.
senses.example: to share a shelter with another

senses.definition: To tell to another.
senses.example: He shared his story with the press.

senses.definition: To allow public or private sharing of resources in a network, or content on social media.
senses.example: to share a folder, a screen

senses.definition: A portion of something, especially a portion given or allotted to someone.
senses.example: Each of the robbers took a share of the loot.

senses.definition: A financial instrument that shows that one owns a part of a company that provides the benefit of limited liability.
A configuration enabling a resource to be shared over a network.
senses.example: Upload media from the browser or directly to the file share.

senses.definition: The action of sharing something with other people via social media.
The cutting blade of an agricultural machine like a plow, a cultivator or a seeding-machine.
The sharebone or pubis.

core.definition: To give part of what you have to someone else so they can use or enjoy it too.

pronunciation.tip: Say a clear, rhotic r at the end, so the word does not turn into "shay". The vowel is the diphthong-free "eh" of "bed" followed by r, so it sounds like "chair" with an sh start.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Sharing usually signals generosity and cooperation, though "share your opinion" or "share the bill" can be neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use share in almost every setting, from kids being told to share toys to colleagues sharing files and friends splitting a dessert. In a restaurant, "We'll share" tells the server you want one plate for two. The verb often takes an object and a preposition phrase, as in "share with" or "share something with someone".

distinctions.note: Divide focuses on splitting something into parts, while share focuses on giving part of it to someone else.
Give implies transferring something permanently, while share often implies that both people keep using it.

examples.everyday: Do you want to share my fries, or should I order my own?
examples.professional: Can you share the revised budget with the team before tomorrow's review?
examples.analytical: Such a theory of justice requires that the goods of a community be shared among its members on grounds that are publicly defensible.

nuance.analogy: Like cutting a pizza: each slice you hand over still belongs to the whole pie, and you keep your own piece too.
nuance.etymology: From Old English scieran, to cut or divide, which is also the root of shear and shard.
common_mistakes: Using share as a noun when you mean a turn, as in saying "It is my share" for "It is my turn".
Saying "share me" instead of "share with me" or "share it with me".

share.etymology: From Middle English *schare*, *schere*, from Old English *sċearu* (“a cutting, shaving, a shearing, tonsure, part, division, share”), from **skaru*, from Proto-Germanic **skarō* (“a division, detachment”), from Proto-Indo-European **ker-* (“to cut, divide”).

conversation.text: Can you share that video with me?
She shared the article on Facebook.
Do you want to share some fries?

senses.definition: To shake nervously, often from fear or horror.
senses.example: On seeing the spider under his pillow, John shuddered.

senses.definition: To vibrate jerkily.
A shivering tremor, often from fear or horror.
senses.example: Seeing the spider under his pillow gave John a shudder.

senses.definition: A moment of almost pleasurable fear; a frisson.

core.definition: To shake or tremble suddenly and involuntarily, usually from fear, cold or disgust.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced r-colored vowel, so say it like 'er' with no separate vowel sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative or unpleasant, suggesting fear, horror or disgust.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I shudder to think' as a common expression of dread or distaste, such as 'I shudder to think what the bill will be.' Shudder is used in everyday speech about cold or disgust, and in writing about fear. A natural reply to the phrase is a sympathetic laugh or a comment on the situation.

distinctions.note: Shiver usually means shaking from cold; shudder is stronger and often from fear or disgust.
Tremble is more general and can describe small movements from nervousness; shudder is a sharper, sudden shaking.

examples.everyday: I shudder when I think about how cold it was on that camping trip.
examples.professional: When I see the deadline on this project, I shudder, because we have not finished the data cleaning.
examples.analytical: The narrator shudders at the moral cost of his victory, and the scene turns on that physical reaction rather than on argument.

nuance.analogy: A shudder is like a sudden jolt of cold water running through your body.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English shuderen, related to Dutch and German words for shake or tremble.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as a full 'der'; it is reduced to a single r-colored vowel.
Using shudder for ordinary cold; shiver is more natural for simple cold.

shudder.etymology: From Middle English *schoderen*, *schuderen*, possibly from Middle Dutch *schudderen* and/or *schodderen*, iterative forms of the verb at hand in, (both “to shake”), from **skuddjan*, from Proto-Germanic **skudjaną*, from Proto-Indo-European **skewdʰ-*.

senses.definition: To avoid, especially persistently; ostracize.
senses.example: Acrophobes shun mountaineering.

senses.definition: To escape (a threatening evil, an unwelcome task etc).
senses.example: I'll shun meeting them for as long as possible.

senses.definition: To screen, hide.
To shove, push.

core.definition: To deliberately avoid a person, thing or activity, often in a way that rejects or excludes.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable, with a short 'u' like 'cup'. Do not lengthen the vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative or disapproving; it suggests intentional rejection or ostracism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shun for deliberate avoidance of people or behavior, such as shunning a friend or shunning gossip. It is more formal than avoid and carries a stronger sense of rejection. In everyday talk people more often say 'avoid' or 'stay away from.' It is commonly used in news and religious contexts.

distinctions.note: Avoid is neutral and everyday; shun implies deliberate, sometimes social rejection.
Ostracize is stronger and means formally excluding someone from a group; shun can be a quieter, personal refusal to associate.

examples.everyday: My uncle has always shunned crowds, so he skipped the family reunion again.
examples.professional: Several managers shun the weekly update meetings, which makes it hard to coordinate the release.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the community shuns those who question its doctrine, using silence as a form of discipline.

nuance.analogy: To shun someone is like closing a door quietly and not opening it again.
nuance.etymology: From Old English scunian, to avoid or flee from.
common_mistakes: Using shun for casual avoidance of a chore; avoid or skip is more natural.
Saying 'shun from' instead of 'shun' alone.

shun.etymology: From Middle English *schonen* (“to decline to do, avoid, fear”), from Old English *sċunian* (“to shun, fear, avoid”), of origin, though probably ultimately connected to the Proto-Indo-European root **kewH-* (“to cover, conceal”) via Proto-Germanic…

senses.definition: A component in a device, or a point in a network, that, if it were to fail, would cause the entire device or network to fail (normally eliminated by adding redundancy).
senses.example: The Jesus nut got its name because it is a single point of failure — if it goes, there's nothing you can do but pray.

senses.definition: A minor mistake that creates a chain reaction.
senses.example: The intact twine in Dylan's beef Wellington was a single point of failure.
